title: The Federalist Paper Analysis
text:
For this project, I decided to complete option A and conduct a hypothesis test simulation study. I will simulate behavior under the null hypothesis analyzing average sentence length of the main authors of the Federalist Papers (Alexander Hamilton and James Madison), which were 85 essays written between 1787-1788 under the pseudonym Publius. As a (former) politics major these papers are important to me, because I had to read all of them in Intro to American Government. For those who are not politics majors, the Federalist Papers were critical to public acceptance of the U.S. Constitution, leading to its eventual ratification. They were written to explain the Constitution and its benefits to the populace. *Note: Although there were three authors, because John Jay only wrote 5 essays he has been excluded from this study.
I am investigating sentence length because it is one indication of writing style, as some people tend to write more “matter-of-fact” and to the point, while others may write “long, beautiful prose”. For those that do not have the time or energy to read the Federalist Papers in their entirety (increasingly common in our 2026 society), I have constructed this analysis to determine the writing style of the authors. For those inspired, I hope this analysis may spark an interest in reading the actual texts.



I will measure the length of sentences by counting words per sentence through a permutation simulation.
Step 1: calculate average sentence length of each essay.
Step 2: compare the average sentence length per essay between Hamilton and Madison.
I will conduct a 2-sided permutation test with a significance level of 0.05 (industry standard in psychology research methods, which I am currently taking)





“Did the main authors of the Federalist Papers, Hamilton and Madison, write sentences of notably different average lengths?”





Null Hypothesis (H0): Hamilton and Madison wrote sentences of the same average length in their papers.
Alternative Hypothesis (H1): Hamilton and Madison wrote sentences of different average lengths in their papers.




I’ve loaded the data from a public GitHub upload by Nicholas Horton.


Show Code
library(FederalistPapers)

data("FederalistPapers")







Show Code
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)

# view datasets in package
data(package = "FederalistPapers")

# combine data
essay_data <- FederalistPapers |>
    filter(
        author == "Hamilton" | author == "Madison",
        str_to_lower(disputed) == "no"
    ) |>
    arrange(paper, line_number) |>
    group_by(paper, author, title) |>
    summarize(
        essay_text = paste(text, collapse = " "),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

head(essay_data)


# A tibble: 6 × 4
  paper author   title                                                essay_text
  <dbl> <chr>    <chr>                                                <chr>     
1     1 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. I. General Introduction               "THE FEDE…
2     6 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. VI. Concerning Dangers from Dissensi… "THE FEDE…
3     7 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. VII. The Same Subject Continued (Con… "THE FEDE…
4     8 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. VIII. The Consequences of Hostilitie… "THE FEDE…
5     9 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. IX. The Union as a Safeguard Against… "THE FEDE…
6    10 Madison  FEDERALIST No. X. The Same Subject Continued (The U… "THE FEDE…


Show Code
table(subset(essay_data, select = author, drop = TRUE))



Hamilton  Madison 
      51       14 







Show Code
sentence_data <- essay_data |>
    mutate(
        sentences = map(
            essay_text,
            ~ str_split(.x, "(?<=[.!?])\\s+")[[1]]
        ) 
    ) |>
    unnest_longer(sentences, values_to = "sentence") |>
    mutate(
        sentence = str_trim(sentence),
        word_count = str_count(sentence, "\\b[[:alpha:]]+\\b")
    ) |>
    filter(word_count > 0)







Show Code
essay_lengths <- sentence_data |>
    group_by(paper, author, title) |>
    summarize(
        average_sentence_length = mean(word_count),
        number_of_sentences = n(),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

head(essay_lengths)


# A tibble: 6 × 5
  paper author   title                average_sentence_len…¹ number_of_sentences
  <dbl> <chr>    <chr>                                 <dbl>               <int>
1     1 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. I. G…                   31.4                  52
2     6 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. VI. …                   26.9                  76
3     7 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. VII.…                   26.5                  88
4     8 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. VIII…                   27.0                  77
5     9 Hamilton FEDERALIST No. IX. …                   29.6                  68
6    10 Madison  FEDERALIST No. X. T…                   32.6                  93
# ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​average_sentence_length




Show Code
#number of papers per author
essay_lengths |>
    count(author)


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  author       n
  <chr>    <int>
1 Hamilton    51
2 Madison     14


Show Code
#summary of average sentence lengths
essay_lengths |>
    group_by(author) |>
    summarize(
        average = mean(average_sentence_length),
        median = median(average_sentence_length),
        .groups = "drop"
    )


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  author   average median
  <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Hamilton    32.4   32.1
2 Madison     32.6   32.4







Show Code
simulate_null <- function(data) {
    shuffled_data <- data |>
        mutate(shuffled_author = sample(author))

    simulated_means <- shuffled_data |>
        group_by(shuffled_author) |>
        summarize(
            avg_length = mean(average_sentence_length),
            .groups = "drop"
        )

    hamilton_avg <- subset(
        as.data.frame(simulated_means),
        shuffled_author == "Hamilton",
        select = avg_length,
        drop = TRUE
    )

    madison_avg <- subset(
        as.data.frame(simulated_means),
        shuffled_author == "Madison",
        select = avg_length,
        drop = TRUE
    )

    simulated_difference <- hamilton_avg - madison_avg

    return(simulated_difference)
}







Show Code
FederalistPapers |>
  filter(author == "Madison") |>
  distinct(paper, disputed) |>
  count(disputed)


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  disputed     n
  <chr>    <int>
1 no          14
2 yes         15







Show Code
set.seed(47)

n_simulations <- 5000

null_differences <- map_dbl(
    1:n_simulations,
    ~ simulate_null(essay_lengths)
)

#qualtiy check
head(pull(sentence_data, sentence), 15)

 [9] "This idea will add the inducements of philanthropy to those of patriotism, to heighten the solicitude which all considerate and good men must feel for the event."                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
[10] "Happy will it be if our choice should be directed by a judicious estimate of our true interests, unperplexed and unbiased by considerations not connected with the public good."

Show Code
ggplot(
    essay_lengths,
    aes(x = author, y = average_sentence_length, fill = author)
) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +
    labs(
        title = "Average Sentence Length by Author",
        subtitle = "One Point Per Essay",
        x = "Author",
        y = "Average Words Per Sentence",
        fill = "Author"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()









Graph Description: The boxplot above compares the average sentence lengths for both Hamilton and Madison across their Federalist papers, with each point representing a single essay. This allows us to analyze who wrote longer sentences in their essays, on average.





Show Code
author_means <- essay_lengths |>
    group_by(author) |>
    summarize(
        avg_length = mean(average_sentence_length),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

hamilton_avg <- subset(
    as.data.frame(author_means),
    author == "Hamilton",
    select = avg_length,
    drop = TRUE
)

madison_avg <- subset(
    as.data.frame(author_means),
    author == "Madison",
    select = avg_length,
    drop = TRUE
)

observed_difference <- hamilton_avg - madison_avg

observed_difference


[1] -0.2016115


Note: Since the observed difference is negative, it indicates that Madison wrote longer sentences on average.





Show Code
#calculate p-value
p_value <- (
    sum(abs(null_differences) >= abs(observed_difference)) + 1
) / (n_simulations + 1)

p_value


[1] 0.8580284







Show Code
null_data <- data.frame(
    difference = null_differences
)

ggplot(null_data, aes(x = difference)) +
    geom_histogram(
        bins = 40,
        fill = "skyblue",
        color = "beige"
    ) +
    geom_vline(
        xintercept = observed_difference, 
        color = "green",
        linetype = "dashed",
        linewidth = 1
    ) +
    geom_vline(
        xintercept = -observed_difference,
        color = "green",
        linetype = "dashed",
        linewidth = 1
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Simulated Difference in Length of Average Sentence Per Author",
        subtitle = "5,000 Permutations (Under the Null)",
        x = "Difference in Average Words Per Sentence",
        y = "Number of Simulations"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()









The above histogram illustrates the distribution of differences in average sentence length from 5,000 simulations under the null hypothesis (“Hamilton and Madison wrote sentences of the same average length in their papers”). For each simulation, the author labels were randomly shuffled to illustrate the differences that may occur if Hamilton and Madison wrote sentences of similar length.
The x-axis shows the difference in average words per sentence, while the y-axis shows the number of simulations which produced each difference. The dashed line on the histogram with the dashed lines representing the observed differences. The green dashed line represents the observed difference and negative observed difference, indicating that any difference between the two authors falling within the lines may have occured by random chance, while those observed differences that fall outside of this boundary are unlikely to be due to chance alone. This visualizes a 2-sided p-value.



The results of my analysis indicated that Hamilton had an average (mean) sentence length of 32 words, and Madison wrote and average of 33 words per sentence. The observed difference between the two was -0.2016, with Madison having the longer sentences on average. Out of the 85 essays making up the Federalist Papers, Hamilton wrote 51 and Madison wrote 14 undisputed e (the 5 by John Jay are not included in this analysis). My permutation test (comparing average sentence length across essays) produced a p-value of 0.86, which fails to reject the null hypothesis.

title: The Federalist Paper Analysis
text:
Final Summary:
For this project, I analyzed the writing patterns for Hamilton’s and Madison’s essays that make up the Federalist Papers. To do this, I cleaned the original data (uploaded by Nicholas Horton), evaluated average sentence length per paper and per author, ran the simulation 5,000 times under the null hypothesis, using the simulation function and mapping, visualizing my findings through a boxplot and histogram. I also calculated the observed difference and p-value for my simulation to determine if there was statistically significant evidence to reject the null (p < 0.05), which turned out to be 0.86 (much larger than 0.05). This indicates there was not a significant difference between the sentence length of both authors.

title: The Speeches of Hamlet
text:
This is a full text analysis project using dialogue from Shakespeare’s play Hamlet. I analyze character strings to answer the following research questions: 1. Who is the biggest yapper (i.e. who talks the most) in Hamlet? 2. How does language about love compare to language about death?




Cleaning data code
library(randomcoloR)
library(tidyverse)
library(forcats)
library(stringr)
library(plotly)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

hamlet <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/hamlet.csv')

hamlet <- hamlet |>
  filter(
    !str_detect(
      character,
      regex("stage direction", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(dialogue), !is.na(character)) |>
  mutate(
    character = str_remove_all(str_trim(character), ":\\s*$")
  )







Creating the yapper database
# Count words in each phrase.
hamlet_words <- hamlet |>
  mutate(
    word_count = str_count(
      dialogue,
      "\\b[[:alpha:]]+\\b"
    )
  )

# Add words per character, per act. 
act_words <- hamlet_words |>
  group_by(act, character) |>
  summarise(
    total_words = sum(word_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )






Creating the yapper visualization
# making the color differences between characters more visible
character_levels <- act_words |>
  group_by(character) |>
  summarise(total = sum(total_words), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(total)) |>
  pull(character)

set.seed(102)
character_colors <- randomcoloR::distinctColorPalette(
  length(character_levels)
)

names(character_colors) <- character_levels

act_plot <- ggplot(
  act_words,
  aes(
    x = act,
    y = total_words,
    fill = fct_reorder(character, -total_words, .fun = sum),
    text = paste0(
      "Act: ", act,
      "<br>Character: ", character,
      "<br>Words: ", total_words
    )
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = character_colors
  ) + 
  labs(
    title = "Who Speaks the Most in Each Act of Hamlet?",
    x = "Act",
    y = "Total Words Spoken",
    fill = "Character"
  ) +
  theme_gray()

ggplotly(act_plot, tooltip = "text")









For Question 1, I used an interactive, plotly stacked bar graph to visualize the characters that speak the most (Hamlet) and the least (Guildenstern). Each bar represents one of the 5 acts in the play. The colors represent each character, and if you click on a character’s name in the key the plot will isolate only their data.
From the bar graphs, you can see that the top 5 biggest yappers are all male characters (Hamlet, King Claudius, Lord Polonius, Horatio, and Laertes), followed by Ophelia in 6th place. What does it say about the focus of this piece that so many lines are spoken by the same 5 men?






Does this play care more about love or revenge (through death)?
love_pattern <- "\\b(love|loves|loved|loving|lover|lovers)\\b"

death_pattern <- "\\b(death|dead|die|dies|died|dying|kill|kills|killed|killing)\\b"

love_death <- hamlet |>
  mutate(
    love_count = str_count(
      str_to_lower(dialogue),
      love_pattern
    ),
    death_count = str_count(
      str_to_lower(dialogue),
      death_pattern
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(act) |>
  summarise(
    Love = sum(love_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    Death = sum(death_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Love, Death),
    names_to = "Theme",
    values_to = "Occurrences"
  )






Show Code
love_you_pattern <-"\\blove\\b(?=\\s+you\\b)"

love_you_count <- hamlet |>
  mutate(
    love_you = str_count(
      str_to_lower(dialogue),
      love_you_pattern
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(character) |>
  summarise(
    total_love_you_pattern = sum(love_you, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(total_love_you_pattern > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(total_love_you_pattern))

love_you_count

  character total_love_you_pattern
  <chr>                      <int>
1 Hamlet                         1







Show Code
behind_love_pattern <- "[[:alpha:]']+(?= love[sdr]?)" #"\\w+(?= love[sdr]?)" didn't allow apostrophes

behind_love_words <- hamlet |>
  mutate(
    words = str_extract_all(
      str_to_lower(dialogue), 
      behind_love_pattern
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(words)

#complete bar chart
behind_love_words |>
  count(words, sort = TRUE) |>
  #dont use slice_max(frequency, n = 15) |>
  head(15) |>
ggplot(
  aes(
    #x = frequency,
    x = reorder(words, n),
    y = n
  )) +
  geom_col(fill = "purple", width = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "15 Most Common Words Appearing Before 'Love' in Hamlet",
    x = "Word",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"), 
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(15, 20, 15, 20)
  ) + 
  coord_flip()














Line chart code
love_death_plot <- ggplot(
  love_death,
  aes(
    x = act,
    y = Occurrences,
    color = Theme,
    group = Theme,
    text = paste0(
      "Act: ", act,
      "<br>Theme: ", Theme,
      "<br>Occurrences: ", Occurrences
    )
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Love vs. Death in Hamlet",
    x = "Act",
    y = "Number of Word Occurrences",
    color = "Theme"
  ) +
  theme_gray()

ggplotly(love_death_plot, tooltip = "text")








Summary table code
act_totals <- love_death |>
  group_by(act, Theme) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Occurrences = sum(Occurrences),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Theme,
    values_from = Total_Occurrences,
    values_fill = 0
  )

knitr::kable(
  act_totals,
  caption = "Love and Death Word Occurrences by Act"
)

overall_totals <- love_death |>
  group_by(Theme) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Occurrences = sum(Occurrences),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  overall_totals,
  caption = "Total Love and Death Word Occurrences in Hamlet"
)



Total Love and Death Word Occurrences in Hamlet


Theme
Total_Occurrences

This analysis compares the frequency of love and death related words across Hamlet’s 5 acts. It counts related terms using word patterns using an interactive plotly line chart.
Act 1 contains an equal amount of love and death (15 occurrences each). However, the theme of love quickly rises throughout Acts II and III. In Act II, the theme of death is at its lowest, but it peaks around the climax of the play in Act IV. Themes of love peak in Act III, right before Ophelia’s death.
I think its interesting how the theme of love peaks and then drops right before the same happens with the theme of death. I wonder if this could indicate the central focus of the story on violence/death > romance, seeing how taking action/revenge in the face of corruption is central to the climax of the piece, while Hamlet’s romance with Ophelia serves to build up to this turning point.

title: The Speeches of Hamlet
text:
Conclusion
While I didn’t go into this project with gender in mind, I found that my data inadvertently highlights disparities between the amount of speech male versus female characters have (see Plot 1). Additionally, the fact that there are 10 more occurrences of death than there are of love indicates a greater focus on the theme of death in the play Hamlet.
